sentences.text: Scientists know this dinosaur from a collection of bones including jaw fragments, teeth, a shoulder blade, vertebrae, ribs, a pubis, heel bones, and a foot bone.
The holotype material represents one of the most complete spinosaurid specimens in the world.
The genus Iberospinus contains only one known species, I. natarioi, known from bones belonging to a single individual.
The first fossil material was found in 1999, followed by expeditions between 2004 and 2008.
Additional material was found in June 2020, leading to the formal description of Iberospinus natarioi as a new genus and species in 2022 by Octávio Mateus and Darío Estraviz-López.
Specimen ML1190 was originally described as a Baryonyx in 2011 but was later identified as a unique species in 2019.
The species name natarioi honors Carlos Natário, who discovered the holotype specimen.
Bone characteristics in the tail and foot suggest Iberospinus may have had a semi-aquatic lifestyle, though lacking extreme adaptations seen in other spinosaurines.
Researchers suggest that juvenile traits retained in adults (paedomorphosis) in Iberospinus may have aided swimming locomotion.
A 2017 study determined that the holotype specimen died between 23 and 25 years old, near its maximum size and skeletal maturity.
Iberospinus reached sexual maturity between 13 and 15 years old, indicated by a slowdown in its growth rate.
Scratches on the bones of Iberospinus may be bite marks left by small scavengers.
Evidence suggests Iberospinus died on land and its bones were transported to the lagoon environment where they were found.
In 2019, researchers placed Iberospinus within Spinosauridae but outside the subfamilies Baryonychinae and Spinosaurinae.
Iberospinus is classified within the family Spinosauridae.

Iberospinus was an extinct spinosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) in Portugal.
Iberospinus lived in a lagoon environment represented by marl rocks in the Papo Seco Formation of Portugal.
Iberospinus lived during the Early Cretaceous, between 129 and 125 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
Iberospinus lived during the Barremian stage, between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago.
Some researchers suggest Iberospinus may be closely related to Baryonychinae because the fossils show certain characteristics of that group.
A 2025 study concluded that Iberospinus is the earliest diverging member of Spinosaurinae, ruling out the possibility that it is the same species as Camarillasaurus.
Researchers Mateus and Estraviz-López suggested in 2022 that the fossil material shows some baryonychine characteristics, implying a closer relationship to that group.
